samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name the same concrete problems and fix them well: autosave with undo, a canonical stored unit, scoped resets moved to Advanced, and task-based grouping. B is a bit stronger on defaults and on shrinking the list, with copy-from-another-hive, a hive-level notification switch and search. A is clearly more honest that it can't know what causes the reviews, and it gives a fuller plan to check after release: tag reviews and tickets, check existing analytics, stage the rollout with named metrics. That outweighs B's edge. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers name the specific problem behaviours and propose autosave, removing the unit-change confirmation, safer scoped resets and grouped settings. A is a little stronger on defaults because it also offers copying alert settings from another hive. B is much better on uncertainty: it admits it hasn't seen the reviews, suggests tagging reviews and checking analytics before shipping, and proposes a staged rollout with specific metrics, including alert mute rate to catch noisy defaults.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name the concrete problem behaviours and propose good fixes for defaults, grouping and saving. B goes further on recoverability: it adds undo toasts, a settings snapshot before reset, in-place sync-failure status and a per-hive reset, and it is more careful in its claims ('can't confirm without the review text'). A has stronger post-release instrumentation but overclaims that the setting order is 'almost certainly the main cause', so B edges it overall. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers name all four problem behaviours, propose sensible default-on alerts with copy-from-hive, switch to save-as-you-go, drop the unit confirmation and move the reset, and group the 38 settings without removing any. A is stronger on recoverability: it adds undo toasts and a settings snapshot so the reset can be undone, and it is careful about thresholds converting correctly when the unit changes. B is stronger on what to watch after release, with instrumentation, a tally of reviews and tickets, and a staged rollout, but it overstates when it calls the ordering 'almost certainly' the main cause.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name the specific problem behaviors and propose autosave, removing the unit-change prompt, moving the reset button and regrouping the settings. It also hedges more honestly and proposes specific post-release checks against a recorded baseline. A opens by saying the changes can be made with reasonable confidence without testing, which overstates certainty, though it does suggest tagging reviews to confirm the cause. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers name the specific problem behaviors and propose autosave, removing the unit confirmation, moving the reset, and grouping the settings. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend three explicit modes, give strong reasons against the timing-based gestures, and admit what modes cost. B handles wrong-mode risk better: it keeps Record off the grid entirely, makes each drag undoable as one unit, uses only one confirmation so people still read it, and keeps the selection when switching modes to cut down on switches. It also ties the modes to the operator's actual workflow (look, change, commit). A adds useful ideas, a show-time lock and a dim-room test plan, but its safeguards are slightly less concrete about separating Record from casual gestures. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend three explicit modes, a persistent indicator that doesn't rely on color alone, defaulting to Select, undo for Paint and a confirmation step for Record. A is a little more concrete: selection carries across modes, Record sits outside the grid so a grid touch can never record a cue, and it states the cost it accepts. B ties its reasoning a little more closely to the live show, with a show-time lock state and a test in a dim room that counts errors. These strengths roughly cancel out, so neither answer is clearly better.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend two explicit modes with a separate Record button and argue well against hidden gestures. A gives more specific show-time safeguards: the paint tool is shown in the mode bar, each stroke is one undo step, and the grid frame changes in a way color-blind operators can read. It also gives a clear reason why overwriting a cue alone needs confirmation. B frankly admits that mode errors happen, but its auto-revert after one stroke would slow painting across many lights, and it wrongly says a stray paint changes all 48 lights. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend two modes plus a separate Record button and explain why hidden long-press timing is risky. B is more specific about show time: it puts the mode where the operator is looking, shows the active paint tool, makes each stroke one undo step, and asks for a named confirmation only when overwriting a cue. A is a bit more upfront about the cost of modes (forgetting which mode you're in) but overstates the risk ("changes 48 lights") and gives fewer concrete safeguards.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend two grid modes, keep Record as a separate action, and add undo and a show lock, so they are very close in substance. A has some extra safeguards: undo that restores the live lights, always reopening in Select, and an 'apply to selection' option. However, A cites an unexplained 'skill's rule' and adds generic accessibility points. B ties its reasoning more tightly to show conditions: it stresses that the operator can always see what the next touch will do, lets Paint switch itself off so it can't be left on by accident, and gives a concrete fallback if switching modes proves too slow. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same recommendation: two grid modes, Select and Paint, with Record as a separate action that needs confirmation, plus undo and a show lock. B goes further on show-time safety. Its undo restores the actual light levels, not just the screen, it confirms only when a cue would be overwritten, it always reopens in Select, and it weighs the cost it accepts (one extra tap during prep) against a wrong look the audience sees. B has two flaws: a stray reference to 'the skill's rule' and a generic point about accessibility. A is tighter but slightly less thorough, and its idea of reverting Paint to Select 'on a lift' would fight against painting by dragging.
